mediaItem.network: Lava for Good podcast in association with signal company number one
mediaItem.seriesType: Episodic Series (based on the format and focus on different cases)
mediaItem.focusTheme_Work: Wrongful convictions, eyewitness misidentification, flaws in the justice system, the Innocence Project.
mediaItem.keyStats: Mistaken eyewitness identification is the leading cause of wrongful convictions. Cross-racial identification is particularly unreliable.
mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode of Wrongful Conviction with Jason Flom features Guy Miles, who was wrongfully convicted of armed robbery and served over 18 years in prison, and Justin Brooks, founder of the California Innocence Project, who helped exonerate him.  Miles recounts his unbelievable story of being convicted based on flawed eyewitness identification despite having an alibi and being in another state when the crime occurred. The podcast highlights the failures of the justice system, including ineffective counsel, suggestive identification procedures, and prosecutorial intransigence even after evidence of innocence emerged.  Brooks details the legal battles and the difficult choices Miles faced, including a plea deal that allowed his release but required him to plead no contest. The episode underscores the devastating impact of wrongful convictions on individuals and families and calls for systemic reform and support for organizations like the California Innocence Project. The importance of eyewitness identification reform and the dangers of plea bargains for innocent individuals are also discussed.

featuredIndividual.exonerationYear: 2016 (released after pleading no contest, conviction reversed by court of appeal prior)
contributingFactorsRaw: Eyewitness misidentification, suggestive photo arrays, ineffective defense counsel, cross-racial identification issues.
featuredIndividual.status: Released after pleading no contest to resolve reprosecution threat; conviction was reversed by the court of appeal. Seeking clemency to address felony status.
innocenceLawyersRaw: Justin Brooks, founder and director of the California Innocence Project, and Alyssa Bjerkhoel (mentioned as "Alyssa"). Described as dedicated and effective, fighting for years through multiple hearings and appeals.
featuredIndividual.narrativeOriginalCrime: A savings and loan in Fullerton, California was robbed by three men. Bernard Teamer, one of the robbers, was quickly apprehended. Guy Miles was mistakenly identified as one of the other robbers despite being in Las Vegas at the time.
keyEvidenceProsecutionRaw: Eyewitness identification by a bank teller. Despite initial uncertainty and later recantation and then re-identification after a recess and seeing a photo.
featuredIndividual.trialDefenderNotes: Frank Williams, the original defense lawyer, was described as "terrible, terrible," unprepared, ineffective, and possibly suspicious in his conduct. He was a family friend hired due to familiarity rather than competence.
keyEvidenceExonerationRaw: Confessions from the actual robbers that Guy Miles was not involved.  Flaws in the photo array identification process were exposed. Nine alibi witnesses from Las Vegas, six of whom testified, placing Miles out of state at the time of the robbery. Court of Appeal reversed the conviction based on insufficient evidence.
featuredIndividual.actualPerpetratorDetails: Bernard Teamer was identified and arrested quickly after the robbery. Two other individuals were involved in the robbery with Teamer, and they later confessed that Guy Miles was not involved. The transcript mentions one suspect described as looking like Warren G.

keyQuotesRaw: Guy Miles: "I've never been in trouble in my life... I was brought up like cops are the good guys." (Beginning, illustrating initial trust in the system)
Guy Miles: "I'm not innocent to approve and guilty, I'm guilty until I approve my innocence and that's absolutely what happened to me." (Describing the burden shift in the justice system)
Justin Brooks on the photo arrays: "It's the most ridiculous set of photo arrays you've ever seen." (Highlighting the flawed identification process)
Assistant DA Karen Walk (reportedly): "I don't believe you did this case, but you're good for it." (Revealing prosecutorial misconduct and focus on conviction over justice)
Guy Miles on prison survival: "I had to basically just trick my mind into believing that I was going to get out tomorrow, the next day soon." (Describing coping mechanisms in wrongful imprisonment)
Justin Brooks on plea deal: "Plea bargains are now defining the entire system... This wasn't true 10, 15 years ago." (Commentary on systemic issues in plea bargaining)

Guy Miles' closing statement: "Continue to fight, continue to keep hope alive, just stay strong and believe not every DA is bad, not every judge is bad, not every lawyer is bad, but we just have to pray and ask God to just continue giving the strength that we do find a good one..." (Message of resilience and hope).
systemicIssuesRaw: Flawed eyewitness identification procedures, especially cross-racial identification.
Suggestive photo arrays and police influence on witness identification.
Ineffective defense counsel and lack of resources for defendants.
Prosecutorial misconduct and focus on conviction rates over justice.
Coercive plea bargain system that pressures innocent people to plead guilty.
Difficulty in overturning wrongful convictions even with strong evidence of innocence.
Trial judges biased against exoneration even after appellate reversal.
District Attorney offices reprosecuting even after exonerations, wasting taxpayer money.
Limitations of clemency process and political nature of pardons.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Reform eyewitness identification procedures to minimize suggestiveness and improve accuracy.
Reduce excessively long sentences that incentivize plea bargains from innocent individuals.
Increase funding and resources for public defenders and innocence projects.
Establish independent conviction review units within prosecutor's offices to proactively address wrongful convictions.
Promote prosecutorial accountability and discourage conviction-at-all-costs mentality.
Encourage citizens to engage in jury duty and become informed about the justice system.
Support organizations like the California Innocence Project.
Call on Governor Jerry Brown to grant clemency to the California 12 and others with strong innocence claims.
personalNarrativeRaw: Guy Miles experienced over 18 years of wrongful imprisonment, losing crucial years with his family, including the birth of his grandson and his daughter's pregnancy.
The wrongful conviction caused immense emotional distress for Guy and his family, particularly his mother, whose health was affected.
Despite the horrific ordeal, Guy maintained hope and resilience, relying on his faith and family support to survive.
Guy's experience highlights the profound and long-lasting damage wrongful convictions inflict on individuals and their loved ones.
His final thoughts emphasize perseverance, faith, and the need for systemic change to prevent future injustices.
